youtube.title: Cause and Effect for Kids: Signal Words and Chain Reactions | Grade 4 Reading | Toy Box Friends
youtube.description:
A domino run rings a bell. But why? Robo and Owl follow the chain backwards and turn reading into detective work.
Kids learn that a cause is why something happens and an effect is what happens; signal words (because, since, due to, so, as a result, therefore), even when the cause comes second in the sentence; chains where one effect becomes the next cause; the lucky socks trap (happening first is not proof); and how to answer with evidence from a nonfiction text about squirrels planting oak forests.
Try at home: keep a chain journal. Draw three dominoes, write what happened today, and ask so what happened next? If you build a real domino run, do it on the floor away from stairs and keep small pieces away from babies.

objects.text: It rained, so the match was cancelled.
The match was cancelled because it rained.
The ground was wet due to the storm.
Turtle was tired, therefore he took a nap.
It rained all night, so the playing field turned into a muddy pond. Because of the mud, the football match was cancelled. Robo had a free morning, so he baked banana bread.
The warm smell drifted out of the window. As a result, Squirrel knocked on the door with a big smile. They shared the bread and played games all afternoon.
In autumn, grey squirrels bury acorns one at a time in many different places. They do this because food is hard to find in winter.
Squirrels dig up many of their acorns later, but they do not come back for all of them. As a result, some forgotten acorns sprout in spring.
Over many years, these little seedlings can grow into tall oak trees. So a squirrel's winter food store helps new forests grow.
Robo forgot to charge his battery.
The alarm clock did not ring, so ...
The road was icy, so the bus drove slowly. What is the cause?
The plant drooped because it got no water. What is the effect?
Why do squirrels bury acorns? Use words from the text.
Robo wore his socks and the team won. Did the socks cause the win?

Cause = why it happened. Effect = what happened.
Signal words: because, since, due to, so, as a result, therefore.
One effect can cause the next: a chain.
Happening first is not proof. Show the evidence!
Chain journal: draw three dominoes. Write something that happened today in the first. Then ask: so what happened next? Underline your signal words.

do.text: Chain Reaction
Watch this. I'll tap the first domino.
Ding! Why did the bell ring?
The marble hit it.
And why did the marble roll?
The last domino pushed it. And each domino pushed the next one.
And why did the first domino fall?
Because I tapped it! Every event has a reason.
Fun fact: a domino can knock over one about one and a half times its size!
A cause is why something happens. Ask: why did it happen?
An effect is what happens. Ask: what happened?
The cause comes first in time. Then the effect. Like a domino push.
The ice pop was left in the sun.
What happened?
It melted! Left in the sun is the cause. Melting is the effect.
Owl practised her spelling words every day.
So I got them all right. Practising was the cause!
The wind blew hard.
So the kite flew high. Cause, then effect.
Quick check! The kite flew high. Is that the cause or the effect?
The effect! It is what happened. The wind was the cause.
Signal words help us find causes and effects.
Because, since and due to point to the cause.
So, as a result and therefore point to the effect.
It rained, so the match was cancelled.
So is the signal word. The cause, it rained, comes first.
The match was cancelled because it rained.
Same events! But now the cause comes second in the sentence.
Which one is the cause?
It rained. The arrow still goes from the cause to the effect.
Order in a sentence is not always order in time.
Some links have no signal word at all. Then ask why.
Your turn. The ground was wet due to the storm. Find the signal word and the cause.
Due to is the signal word. It points to the cause: the storm.
Turtle was tired, therefore he took a nap. Signal word and effect?
Therefore points to the effect: he took a nap.
Here's my rainy Saturday. Each event is a domino. Let's read it in short lines.
It rained all night, so the playing field turned into a muddy pond.
Because of the mud, the football match was cancelled.
Robo had a free morning, so he baked banana bread.
The warm smell drifted out of the window.
As a result, Squirrel knocked on the door with a big smile.
They shared the bread and played games all afternoon.
rain → mud → no match → free → bread → smell → visit
One effect became the next cause. That's a chain!
Wait. Robo had a free morning. There is no signal word. Why did he have a free morning?
Because the match was cancelled! The cause is in the sentence before.
I wore my striped socks, and my team won. The socks made us win!
Did the socks cause the win, or did the win just happen after?
Evidence one: last week you wore the same socks, and your team lost.
Hmm. Same socks, different result.
Evidence two: your team practised passing all week. That is why you won.
So happening first is not proof. Before is not always because!
before ≠ because
Hi! I'm a grey squirrel. Let's read about me!
In autumn, grey squirrels bury acorns one at a time in many different places.
They do this because food is hard to find in winter.

do.words: because food is hard to find in winter

do.text: Why do squirrels bury acorns? Show me the evidence.
The text says: because food is hard to find in winter.
Squirrels dig up many of their acorns later, but they do not come back for all of them.
As a result, some forgotten acorns sprout in spring.

do.words: some forgotten acorns sprout in spring

do.text: What happens to forgotten acorns? Some sprout in spring!
Over many years, these little seedlings can grow into tall oak trees.
So a squirrel's winter food store helps new forests grow.
Fun fact: one grey squirrel can bury thousands of nuts in one autumn!
One cause can have two effects. Burying acorns gives the squirrel winter food.
And it helps new oak trees grow. Jays bury acorns too!
Push the first and watch it go!
Because, because, and so, and so!
Why did it happen?
Why did it happen?
The cause!
What happened?
What happened?
The effect!
Move along! Stand tall like a domino. Lean, and sit down on every so!
Match it! Causes are on the left. Effects are on the right, all mixed up.
The snow kept falling. What happened?
Robo forgot to charge his battery. What happened?
The puppy chewed the shoe. What happened?
The plant got no water. What happened?
Challenge! The alarm clock did not ring, so what happened next? Think of two links.
so ... so ...
Here's one idea. Owl woke up late, so she ran to the bus!
Or: Owl woke up late, so she missed breakfast, so her tummy rumbled all morning!
Every link answers the question: so what happened next?
One: the road was icy, so the bus drove slowly. What is the cause?
The road was icy. That's why the bus drove slowly.
Two: the plant drooped because it got no water. What is the effect?
The plant drooped. That's what happened.
Three: why do squirrels bury acorns? Use words from the text.
Because food is hard to find in winter.
Four: Robo wore his socks and the team won. Did the socks cause the win?
No. The win came after, not because. Practice caused the win.
